Brazil synthetic analysis · Physical climate risk driven by peer-reviewed climate data.

A bank's physical climate risk depends on the assets and activities behind its lending. This case follows a Brazilian credit book through reporting location, physical losses, portfolio tails and credit outcomes, showing how quantitative climate information can support lending decisions.

This case study applies real climate datasets and quantitative risk modelling to a synthetic banking book. Clients can replace the example borrower, asset, loan and financial inputs with accurate data from their own portfolio to assess their physical climate risk.

Find the analysis in the Alpha-Klima GitHub repository, under notebooks/99_case_studies. This companion explains selected results, the information behind them and how clients can apply the workflow to their own exposures.

A small book with different operating exposures

The example links six borrowers, twelve loans and ten financed sites, with R$ 971 million drawn. The sites include grain warehouses, transport terminals, cotton, cocoa and ethanol mills, and an administrative office. Each borrower has working-capital lending and a longer investment loan.

Each activity connects climate to a different part of the business. Flood damages exposed stock, machinery and buildings; heat reduces working capacity or increases cooling demand. Linking a loan to the activity it finances identifies the physical effects that can affect its borrower, alongside the loan's balance and maturity.

The asset register makes that connection. It records site locations, activities, values and operating inputs and links them to borrowers and loans. Clients use these records to follow the same exposure from the reporting tables through physical-loss estimates and the credit calculation.

Financed locations reveal where exposure belongs

The first step compares reporting exposure at borrower headquarters (Nível 3) and at financed activities (Nível 1). It uses AdaptaBrasil's municipal drought and intense-rain indicators within the CRFR2 physical-risk tables of Brazil's GRSAC disclosure framework.

A headquarters address locates the company; financed sites locate its productive activities. A warehouse or mill can operate hundreds of kilometres from the head office, in a different climate and economic region. Assigning lending to the financed location connects the reported exposure to the activity supporting repayment.

This location choice moves R$ 290.4 million—30% of drawn exposure—to another macro-region. Nine disclosed risk classes change, and six other cells become populated or empty. The comparison holds lending amounts and climate datasets constant, isolating the effect of locating the financed activities.

For financing with an identified activity, the reporting location follows that activity's municipality. When a borrower has several sites, clients allocate exposure according to the activities supported by each loan. This gives the reporting tables a consistent link to the client's actual lending.

Municipal context becomes an asset-level assessment

Site coordinates add detail within the municipal picture. A riverside terminal and an asset on higher ground can share a municipal flood-threat class while facing different depths. Municipal indicators support regional screening and disclosure; coordinate readings connect hazard intensity and frequency to the financed location.

AdaptaBrasil summarises conditions at municipal level. The asset-level assessment asks how deep a flood can be, how often it occurs, or how much heat exceeds an operating threshold. These physical quantities provide the inputs for vulnerability models and financial calculations tied to a particular asset.

Dataset resolution sets the spatial detail available at the coordinates. Site elevation, first-floor height and protection then connect the gridded water level to the building. Accurate site information lets the assessment distinguish the hazard around the asset from the conditions the asset itself experiences.

Scenarios show change relative to a baseline

Scenarios describe future climate conditions under specified pathways and horizons. Both AdaptaBrasil and Alpha-Klima use them to compare future exposure with a baseline. Comparing pathways shows how risk develops under different futures; comparing with the baseline identifies the additional change alongside the risk already present.

Read every result with its scenario and reference period. The headline heat and water-stress results use SSP5-8.5, while flood uses RCP8.5. Selected hazards also have lower-emission comparisons. Flood starts from the projected 2030 slice; heat uses the historical 2005 slice. These years represent climate periods, rather than individual calendar-year forecasts.

The river depth with a 1% annual chance in 2030 occurs 1.5–2.2 times as often by 2080 under RCP8.5 at the exposed sites. On the coast, the corresponding depth occurs about 8–9 times as often by 2050 at the central sea-level estimate. Following a fixed depth shows how the probability of a damaging event changes.

Water stress shows why the starting level matters. A coastal warehouse's ratio grows more than fourfold by 2050 but remains in the low–medium class. Read the change alongside the absolute level to understand its significance. Historical drought readings provide current context; future drought sits outside this comparison. Each indicator describes a specific process.

Heat assessment connects temperature and humidity with work intensity and operating thresholds. These inputs distinguish working conditions at a mill from cooling demand at an office. Clients can use the relevant site readings to identify which activities require closer financial assessment.

Hazard, exposure and vulnerability give risk its meaning

Hazard × exposure × vulnerability connects the climate event, the assets or activities exposed and their response. Vulnerability models convert the relevant hazard into damage, working-time loss or additional energy use. Asset values and operating costs express those physical effects in money.

Asset-specific modelling makes the financial consequence depend on the financed business. The same flood depth affects different amounts of stock and equipment; the same heat affects manual work and an air-conditioned office differently. Asset characteristics determine the response, and exposure determines its financial scale. Clients supply the site and operating information needed for that connection.

The monetary results cover hazards with a matching impact model. Drought and water stress remain hazard indicators in this example, with their financial consequences outside the priced channels. Their readings still help identify water-dependent operations that warrant further investigation.

Heat costs concentrate in the mills

Under SSP5-8.5, producing sites add an estimated R$ 9.25 million in annual heat productivity cost by 2050, about 0.53% of their revenue. Three mills contribute 94% of that amount. Labour costs and the mix of heat-exposed tasks connect working-time loss to each site's operations. The office's heat impact enters through cooling demand.

Under SSP2-4.5, additional productivity cost reaches about R$ 7.1 million in 2050. Comparing the two pathways shows the larger increase under the higher-emission case. Comparing sites identifies the mills as the main contributors, directing attention to the workforce and operating conditions behind that concentration.

Existing flood loss and future increments answer different questions

Coastal expected annual damage adds R$ 6.71 million between 2030 and 2050 across two sites, mainly at the port terminal. River damage adds R$ 7.23 million between 2030 and 2080 across six sites, with the river terminal contributing the largest increase.

Read the baseline alongside the increment. The coastal warehouse already has an estimated annual mean loss of about 22% of its example value in 2030. The terminal contributes the largest future increase. These two views identify existing exposure and the additional burden from changing climate conditions.

Elevation, protection and vulnerability connect water depth to damage. The river estimate scales baseline damage with ground-adjusted depth growth, holding baseline vulnerability fixed. Read the selected annual increments with their available horizons and baselines. The portfolio analysis then estimates how losses occur together in a joint annual distribution.

Portfolio aggregation makes shared losses visible

Portfolio aggregation assesses how much loss can occur across the financed sites in the same year. A flood footprint can reach several assets, and nearby operations can share a climate event. Correlation between their losses affects the probability of a severe portfolio outcome, making location and event footprints relevant to the combined risk.

Expected losses can be summed, while portfolio percentiles require the joint loss distribution. Shared events reduce the diversification implied by treating every site independently. At the other extreme, assuming every site suffers its worst loss together overstates concentration. Explicit dependence assumptions connect individual loss estimates to the portfolio's actual pattern of shared exposure.

This matters most when assessing the tail: infrequent, severe losses relevant to resilience and capital planning. Portfolios with similar average losses can have different tails because their assets share different events. Asset-level assessment identifies the exposures; aggregation describes their combined extreme outcomes and the concentration a lender needs to consider.

The Alpha-Klima portfolio service groups sites that can share a hazard footprint and aggregates their losses. Expected annual physical loss rises from R$ 44.5 million historically to R$ 52.8 million in 2050 and R$ 55.3 million in 2080 under its SSP5-8.5 scenario label. The 99.9th-percentile loss rises from R$ 182.8 million to R$ 198.0 million by 2080.

Read average and severe-year losses together when considering financial burden and the capacity to absorb a shock. Clusters identify which exposures contribute to the same event. The portfolio service uses its own hazard coverage and scenario mapping. The credit example below separately combines flood frequency, damage and borrower credit inputs to estimate default and credit losses.

Quantified physical risk can inform credit models

Quantitative physical-risk inputs connect climate to a borrower's ability to repay and the bank's recovery after default. Flood frequency describes the event's probability; damage describes its effect on borrower assets. Combined with existing credit parameters, these inputs allow a bank to assess how physical risk changes its credit outcomes.

The example follows BIS Working Paper 1274, Incorporating physical climate risks into banks' credit risk models. The paper extends a one-factor credit model with a climate event that reduces borrower asset value. The notebook applies that framework to flood probabilities, damage estimates and borrower inputs.

Probability of default (PD) describes the chance of default. Loss given default (LGD) describes the share of exposure lost after recovery. Exposure at default (EAD) includes outstanding balances and relevant undrawn commitments. Model risk-weighted assets (RWA) express the risk-adjusted exposure for the capital calculation. The example compares unchanged recovery with LGD increasing alongside flood damage.

The selected flood curves cover five borrowers and R$ 787 million of EAD, about 75% of total EAD. Both horizons use these same borrowers. Within the paper's framework, each borrower represents a granular portfolio of similar loans. Read the credit results within this coverage and model interpretation.

Change in model risk-weighted assets (RWA), RCP8.5 with the central coastal sea-level estimate. Both years cover the same five borrowers; each recovery case is compared with its own 2030-frequency baseline.
HorizonLGD unchangedDamage-linked LGD
2050+4.9%+6.0%

C03 has the largest annual PD increase, from 3.32% to 4.41% by 2080, while its model RWA changes little. The default probability and extreme credit-loss calculation measure different outcomes. Reading them together helps a lender distinguish expected credit burden from the severe losses relevant to capital.

The 2080 credit calculation uses the last supported coastal event frequency, from 2050. The notebook documents its reference event and dependence assumptions. Clients apply the same framework using accurate borrower asset values, volatility and baseline credit parameters, connecting the climate inputs to their own book.

Loan timing determines which climate is encountered

Loan maturity determines the climate period a facility encounters. Most loans originated in 2028 mature before 2080, so the notebook compares the same loan sizes and tenors originated later. It tracks repayment over each loan's life, isolating how future climate conditions affect an otherwise comparable lending decision.

Additional lifetime expected credit loss for loans with flood curves (75% of EAD), using damage-linked LGD, relative to the same loans with flood frequency held at its 2030 level.

Read these percentages as increases in lifetime expected credit loss. The calculation sums annual expected losses over repayment without discounting. Comparing origination years connects climate horizons with loan maturity, renewal and future lending, showing which decisions encounter the changing risk over their lives.

From a reporting address to a lending decision

The workflow connects financed locations, operating conditions, shared events and credit inputs. Location identifies the exposure; asset characteristics translate hazards into losses; aggregation captures severe portfolio outcomes; and borrower parameters and loan timing connect physical risk to credit decisions.

Clients can use this sequence to identify where better site information improves the assessment, which operations contribute most to loss and which exposures share severe events. The resulting quantitative inputs support a review of physical climate risk within the bank's credit framework.

Read and adapt the notebook

Start with setup and inputs, then follow reporting location, hazards, physical impacts, aggregation and credit. Figure numbers in this companion identify the supporting results. The notebook includes additional scenarios, site tables and exported outputs for investigating the findings and comparing client exposures.

Replace the example registers under resources/brazil. Use Run settings to choose the assessment, Values to replace to enter client parameters and The book's inputs to load the registers. The following information connects each part of the analysis:

  • Borrowers and loans: link borrowers, facilities and financed sites; supply drawn and undrawn balances, exposure allocation, baseline PD and LGD, and loan origination, repayment and maturity.
  • Assets and operations: supply coordinates, municipality, activity and vulnerability characteristics, asset values, elevation and floor height, revenues, heat-exposed work, labour costs, cooling use and electricity prices.
  • Assessment choices: select pathways, horizons, baselines, reference flood events and sea-level assumptions, and provide borrower asset volatility and relevant credit parameters.

Use accurate data for the client's assets and credit book, and keep the identifiers linking borrowers, loans and sites consistent. Follow the repository's setup and API-access instructions, then rerun the notebook in order after changing inputs or settings. Compare matching horizons, coverage and baselines. The platform documentation provides detailed API functions and methods; the platform page and climate-risk FAQs provide broader explanations.

Sources and data

The portfolio records and financial parameters are example inputs. Climate data come from scientific reanalysis and climate-model projections, including ERA5-Land, WRI Aqueduct and datasets distributed through OS-Climate. Alpha-Klima processes these into hazard indicators and asset impacts. The notebook identifies the exact datasets, models, units, scenarios and horizons used in the results.

  • Climate and impacts: ERA5-Land research, WRI Aqueduct Floods methodology, SPEI, and OS-Climate hazard data. The platform's hazard inventory and vulnerability documentation provide further detail after sign-in.
  • Municipal reporting: AdaptaBrasil methodology and the BCB GRSAC layouts.
  • Credit methodology: BIS Working Paper 1274, which connects physical climate events with default and credit-loss distributions.
